title: 5 crush grip Mistakes That Are Destroying Your hand tendons
description: Your crush training might be quietly taxing the very tendons it should build. Run the thirty-second diagnostic, then meet the five mistakes - the bent pulley, the half rep and three more - that separate hands that last from hands that complain.

scenes.narration: Before the mistakes, the diagnostic. Ball in your weaker hand, wrist straight, arm at your side. Thirty seconds: as many crushes as you can - but today, a rep only counts if the ball goes fully flat AND your hand opens fully afterward. Count the honest ones. This stricter count is your real crush number, and it is probably lower than the number you would have claimed yesterday. That gap is not an embarrassment. It is a measurement of how much of your training has been leaking into the five mistakes we are about to name. Keep the honest number. By the end of this episode you will know exactly which mistakes were taxing your tendons - and every one of them is free to fix.

scenes.label: THE LINE FOR AN HONEST CRUSH
scenes.sub: under 15: mistakes are eating you - 15 to 30: building - over 30: clean power
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Thirty honest crushes in thirty seconds - one full, clean rep per second - is where crush power becomes real. Under fifteen, do not reach for a harder ball or a longer program. Your number is being eaten by technique, and technique is the cheapest thing in this entire episode to fix. Between fifteen and thirty, the machinery is sound and the mistakes are occasional visitors - fatigue invites them in during the last ten seconds, which is where your attention should live. Over thirty honest reps, your crush is clean power: full range, straight wrist, both directions of the hand working as one system. Hold your number up against the five mistakes coming. Most men find two of their own in the list. Finding them is not the bad news. The bad news was training them for a year without knowing.

Quick anatomy, so the mistakes make sense. Your fingers are closed by forearm muscles pulling long tendons through your wrist and along your palm. Those tendons run through sheaths and around the wrist's corner like cables in a conduit - a system built for enormous mileage at sensible loads. Tendons are living tissue: loaded well, they thicken and stiffen across months; loaded badly, they do not tear dramatically - they complain, thicken in the wrong way, and start taxing every grip with friction and ache. Here is the principle under all five mistakes: tendons do not care about your intentions, only your doses and your angles. Every mistake ahead is a dosing error or an angle error - too much, too bent, too one-sided, too often, or too unbalanced. Fix the dose and the angle, and the same training that was taxing your cables starts building them.

One more piece of science before the list: tendons keep office hours. After a heavy loading session, a tendon's rebuilding runs for a day or two, and loading it maximally again inside that window spends tissue faster than the rebuild replaces it. This is why the fifth mistake - training crush hard every day - is on a list about destruction, even though the training itself is 'just squeezing a ball'. Muscles forgive daily enthusiasm. Tendons invoice it. The flip side is hopeful: dosed correctly - hard days spaced, angles clean, both directions trained - hand tendons become some of the most durable structures you own, outlasting the muscles that pull them. The five mistakes are simply the five ways home trainers accidentally break the dosing rules. Read yours, fix them in order, and your crush count will rise on the same training that was previously taxing you.

Preview the worst offender, because it hides inside good intentions: the bent wrist. Every degree your wrist folds forward during a crush, your tendons pay a friction tax around the corner of the wrist - and the tax is charged on every single rep. A man doing everything else right with a bent wrist is sanding his cables a hundred times a session and calling it training. Watch for it in the list as mistake two, and notice its disguise: it arrives with fatigue, when the squeeze gets desperate and the whole arm starts helping. The fix costs nothing - a straight wrist, checked in a mirror for one session, becomes the default within a week. That is the theme of this whole episode. Your tendons are not being destroyed by hard training. They are being taxed by small, free-to-fix errors, repeated faithfully.

The skinny advantage in a mistakes episode is simple: your errors are cheaper to find. Your loads are modest, so a month of imperfect crushing has taxed your tendons lightly compared to a heavy-handed man grinding the same mistakes at twice the force. And your feedback is clearer - you can see the wrist bend, watch the ball stop flattening, feel which hand is being skipped. Men with more insulation guess. You audit. There is a second edge: because your absolute loads are lower, you can rebuild technique at full quality immediately, today, with the same ball - no deload, no layoff, no drama. The five fixes ahead are not a rehab program. They are a software update, and your system can install it this afternoon.

beats.text: YOUR ERRORS COST LESS SO FAR

scenes.narration: We install the update together. Four rounds, alternating hands. Every rep: wrist straight, ball fully flat, hand fully open. Slow enough to be perfect. If a rep breaks a rule, it does not count - and not counting it IS the exercise.

Here they are - the five mistakes, in the order to fix them. Mistake one: half reps. The ball never fully flattens, the hand never fully opens, and the tendons train a shortened, lazier range while the count inflates. Mistake two: the bent wrist - the friction tax from the preview, charged on every rep. Mistake three: strong-hand-only training, which builds a champion and a passenger and calls the average a grip. Mistake four: max crushing every day, invoiced by tendons that needed their rest days - heavy crush work belongs two or three times a week, with the easy days between. Mistake five: never training the opening - crush without spread is a one-country forearm, and the imbalance bill always arrives at the elbow. Five mistakes, five free fixes, and your honest count from the test will rise on exactly the same effort. That is the best deal in this entire season.

scenes.label: WHAT YOUR HONEST NUMBER MEANS
scenes.sub: under 15: taxed - 15 to 30: building - over 30: clean
scenes.narration: So what does your honest count mean? Under fifteen, your tendons are being taxed by technique, not by training - and that is the most hopeful score on the board, because the fix is free and immediate. Between fifteen and thirty, you are building a real crush with occasional leaks; your homework is the last ten seconds of every set, where the mistakes clock in. Over thirty honest reps, your crushing is clean power - full range, straight pulley, both hands, dosed like a professional. Retest the diagnostic in thirty days, same strict rules. Comment your honest count below - and name the mistake that was yours. I will go first in spirit: everybody who has ever trained grip has owned at least two of the five.

Your tendons were never the problem. Your doses and angles were, and those are yours to command. Fix the five, keep the training, and the same work starts building instead of taxing. Thirty days, then we count honestly again. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
